query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear performance of high‐entropy alloy protective coatings is governed by the formation of a continuous, thermally stable spinel oxide layer (e.g., (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4) during high‐temperature exposure. This protective layer forms preferentially in coatings with an equiatomic, homogeneous distribution of elements and acts as a barrier to mechanical wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A microwave-cladded high-entropy alloy coating (Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20) on SS-304 steel with a uniform, equiatomic microstructure.
generation.intervention: Prepare an otherwise identical coating but with a deliberately imbalanced elemental composition (for example, increasing Fe to 30% and reducing the other elements to 17.5% each) to disrupt the uniform formation of the protective oxide layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear testing conditions (e.g., exposure to ~800 °C, sliding speed ~2 m/s, applied load ~15 N, sliding distance ~1000 m) where oxide formation is expected to occur.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or disruption) of a continuous, protective spinel oxide layer, most notably (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4, on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, the homogeneous, equiatomic coating undergoes selective oxidation that uniformly forms a protective spinel oxide film. This film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding wear, thereby lowering wear rates. A disruption in the elemental balance impedes the development of a uniform oxide layer, leading to increased wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The balanced, equiatomic coating will display lower wear rates and a more stable friction coefficient, as confirmed by continuous oxide layer formation. In contrast, the imbalanced coating will show higher wear rates and less continuous oxide coverage.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the equiatomic Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 coating, which under the reported test conditions exhibits a low wear rate (e.g., around 0.0018 mm³/m) and forms a continuous protective oxide layer after high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The effect is hypothesized to hold under high-temperature (near 800 °C) sliding and load conditions with compositions similar to the studied HEA. Its applicability outside this temperature range or with radically different alloying elements is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the oxide layer formation and the potential contributions from other microstructural features (such as secondary intermetallic phases) are not fully quantified and may also affect wear performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings on SS-304: one with the balanced equiatomic composition (Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20) and another with a controlled imbalance (e.g., 30% Fe, 17.5% each Co, Ni, Mn, Cu). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature wear tests (800 °C, 2 m/s sliding speed, 15 N load, 1000 m sliding distance). Analyze the surfaces before and after testing.
measurements: Wear loss measured by profilometry or 3D microscopy
Friction coefficient recorded during wear testing
Surface and cross-sectional oxide layer continuity assessed via SEM/EDS and XRD
Microstructural analysis pre- and post-test to evaluate oxide formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the imbalanced coating exhibits wear rates and oxide layer characteristics (continuity and protective nature) similar to or better than the balanced coating, then the role of the continuous protective oxide layer as the primary governing mechanism for wear resistance would be falsified.
